entries.title: Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry
entries.summary: Hardcoded tool wiring breaks down as an agent's catalog grows from a handful of tools to hundreds. This post walks through a runtime Discover, Instantiate, Execute loop built on AWS Agent Registry, where an orchestrator discovers MCP servers and A2A agents through semantic search at runtime instead of compiling every tool at build time.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry

Runtime discovery with AWS Agent Registry can help address a problem that agent demos might hide. Hardcoded tools work fine for a handful, start to degrade at a few dozen, and become unmanageable beyond that. Enterprise systems expose hundreds of internal APIs for pricing, support, orders, inventory, and customer data. In these systems, the model can spend more tokens disambiguating tool names than reasoning about the user’s request. Each new capability requires a code change in the orchestrator, a redeploy, and a coordinated release across teams that would much rather ship on their own cadence.

This pattern can arise across enterprise software as a service (SaaS) engagements where teams expose large internal API surfaces to agentic consumers. Build-time wiring can become a bottleneck as the catalog expands. One approach is to change how the orchestrator accesses its tools: instead of compiling every tool into the agent, the agent can discover relevant tools at runtime.

AWS Agent Registry is a managed service for cataloging and discovering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agents, and agent skills. Publishers register protocol-specific descriptors and searchable descriptions. At runtime, an orchestrator can search approved, discoverable records and use the returned endpoint and descriptor content to construct a client. Registry search results do not return the capability’s invocation credentials or authentication scheme.

This post walks through the Discover → Instantiate → Execute loop demonstrated by the refactored Python sample. The code deploys an order-management MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, two agent-to-agent (A2A) agents on AgentCore runtime, a Registry, and an orchestrator. The sample directory contains the deployment script, orchestrator, helper modules, and cleanup script.

Solution overview: discover, instantiate, execute

The orchestrator agent in this sample has no built-in knowledge of tools or agents.

Discover

The orchestrator sends a natural-language query to the AWS Agent Registry data plane. The search response includes record identity, name, description, record type, status, version, and protocol descriptors such as MCP server metadata or an A2A agent card. It does not include invocation credentials. The application must obtain and apply the appropriate credentials through a separate, trusted configuration path.

Instantiate

For each returned record, the orchestrator constructs a client from the descriptor type. In this sample, the registered MCP server represents tools that were first added as targets to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The MCP descriptor therefore points to the Gateway endpoint. The orchestrator fetches a Cognito OAuth access token separately and uses it when creating the 

MCPClient
. A2A records contain an agent card whose URL identifies an AgentCore runtime endpoint. The wrapper invokes that runtime through the boto3 data-plane client, which signs the request with the caller’s AWS credentials. Registry discovery supplies connection metadata, not the authentication material.

Execute

An ephemeral inner agent is built with only the dynamically-discovered tools. The large language model (LLM) picks the right one(s) for the request, and the result is synthesized back to the user. After the turn finishes, the inner agent and its clients are torn down. The next request gets a fresh search and a fresh tool set.

The reference architecture used in the sample includes AWS Agent Registry, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Cognito, AWS Lambda, and AWS Secrets Manager.

  • AWS Agent Registry provides the governed, searchable catalog queried by the orchestrator. Only records that complete the configured approval workflow are available through the discoverable data plane.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway exposes the order-management Lambda tools as an MCP server. The sample configures Cognito JWT authorization for inbound Gateway calls and uses the Gateway AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to invoke the Lambda target.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the orchestrator and the Pricing and Customer Support A2A agents. Runtime invocations use IAM-authorized Boto3 calls.
  • Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation model (FM) used by the orchestrator and A2A agents. The sample currently configures an Anthropic Claude Sonnet model through a cross-Region model ID. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

Three demo scenarios exercise the discovery loop with different capability combinations. The first is an MCP-only call (order status). The second chains MCP + A2A (pricing and discounts). The third tests a pure semantic match against ambiguous user intent: return and refund, where those words don’t appear in the matched A2A agent’s name.

Technical implementation

The linked runtime-discovery sample deploys the dependencies, creates and populates the Registry, verifies discovery, deploys the orchestrator, and runs three demos. orchestrator_agent.py contains the per-request discovery loop. utils.py parses Registry descriptors and creates MCP and A2A clients. cleanup.py removes resources.

1. The registration model

A Registry record contains a searchable description plus a protocol-specific descriptor. The sample uses the Agent Registry control-plane client for Registry and record lifecycle operations and the Agent Registry data-plane client for runtime discovery.

Creating a Registry with manual approval and IAM authorization.

The 

recordType
field is required when creating a record. In this sample, MCP servers use 
recordType="MCP"
and A2A-backed agents use 
recordType="AGENT"
. Protocol metadata is stored under 
mcpServer
or 
a2aAgentCard
in the 
descriptors
object. An MCP descriptor contains server metadata and tool definitions. An A2A descriptor contains the agent card. The descriptors contain connection metadata but not the credentials that a consumer must present when invoking the capability.

Building current public-SDK descriptor shapes for MCP and A2A records.

Write descriptions in user-facing language that distinguishes the capability from neighboring records. Descriptor content supplies the protocol-specific server, tool, or agent-card data. Search quality should be evaluated with representative queries. This post does not assume that catalog growth automatically improves ranking.

Creating a Registry record with the current control-plane shape.

2. Approval workflow

With 

autoApproval
set to false, a new record must move from 
DRAFT
to 
PENDING_APPROVAL
and then 
APPROVED
. The submit and status-update actions are IAM-authorized, allowing publisher and approver permissions to be separated. Only approved records are returned by the discoverable Registry data plane.

The two-step approval transition.

3. The discovery layer

The data-plane client supports hybrid keyword and semantic search across discoverable records. The latest method name is search_discoverable_registry_records. Results expose normalized record fields and discoverable descriptors. They don’t expose the capability’s invocation credentials.

Searching approved, discoverable records across protocols.

In the sample scenario, a return-and-refund query retrieves the Customer Support Agent because its description captures that intent. Treat this as a demo result, not a general claim that ranking improves merely because the catalog is larger.

4. The orchestrator

The orchestrator is a Strands agent deployed to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. It exposes 

discover_and_execute
, which searches the Registry, parses each returned descriptor, creates the corresponding MCP or A2A client, and builds a request-scoped inner agent from only those discovered capabilities.

The core of 

discover_and_execute
fits in a single code block:

The orchestrator’s discover/instantiate/execute loop.

The sample fans out several search queries to improve recall for its order-management domain, deduplicates records, and tears down MCP clients after the request. That fan-out is a sample-specific orchestration choice, not a Registry requirement. Authentication remains outside discovery: the Gateway OAuth token is obtained from Cognito configuration and Secrets Manager, whereas A2A runtime calls are signed through the boto3 session.

5. Running the three demos

Each demo exercises a different shape of the discovery loop.

Demo 1: Order status (MCP only)

A request that resolves to a single MCP tool call.

The Registry returns the order management MCP server. The orchestrator calls 

get_order_status
through Gateway, the LLM synthesizes a human-readable response, and the inner agent terminates. No A2A involvement on this turn.

Demo 2: Pricing and discounts (MCP + A2A)

A request that resolves to a multi-protocol chain.

The Registry returns the order management MCP server and the pricing A2A agent: two protocols, one natural-language query. The LLM calls 

get_order_status
to fetch line items, then calls the pricing agent on runtime for discount analysis, then synthesizes a single recommendation.

Demo 3: Return and refund (semantic match)

A request whose intent is not literally present in any tool name.

This demo shows the value of semantic discovery. The phrase ‘return refund’ doesn’t appear in the Customer Support Agent’s registered name. The hybrid search ranks it highly because its description captures the intent. Without Registry, the orchestrator would need hardcoded knowledge of which agent handles returns.

6. Observability

Instrument the discovery and invocation path using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability and Amazon CloudWatch where appropriate. Useful signals include Registry search success and failure, selected record identifiers, client-construction errors, downstream invocation outcomes, end-to-end trace correlation, and application errors. The sample grants Amazon CloudWatch Logs permissions, but it doesn’t create custom metrics or dashboards. Production teams should define the traces, logs, and alerts required for their operating model. Production deployments should also apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a standard control on agent responses.

What teams gain from governed runtime discovery

After the discovery loop is in place, several capabilities that were previously coupled to orchestrator releases become independent.

  • Decoupled publishing. Teams can deploy and register their own MCP servers, agents, and skills. Approval policy determines when a published record becomes available to consumers.
  • No orchestrator code change for newly approved records. In this pattern, adding a compatible, approved Registry record doesn’t require adding a tool-specific import or endpoint to the orchestrator. Changes to protocols, authentication setup, or orchestration policy can still require code or configuration updates.
  • Governed discovery. With manual approval, only reviewed and approved records become discoverable. IAM permissions can separate record publishers from approvers.
  • Separated authentication. Registry authorization can use IAM or custom JWT. Capability invocation authentication is separate: the sample uses Cognito OAuth for Gateway and Boto3/IAM signing for AgentCore runtime. Search results don’t return those credentials.
  • Catalog search instead of prompt stuffing. With hybrid Registry search, the orchestrator retrieves a small candidate set instead of placing the full catalog in the model context. Search quality depends on descriptions, descriptor quality, query design, and evaluation.

When not to use runtime discovery

Runtime discovery is not necessary for every workload. Two patterns can still favor explicit build-time wiring:

  • Small, stable catalogs. If the complete capability set is small and changes rarely, explicit build-time wiring might be simpler and avoid an additional discovery request.
  • Fixed pipelines. When the same capabilities always run in a fixed order, implementing them as a deterministic flow is more straightforward and keeps tracing focused.

Conclusion

Discovery of assets from Registry at runtime makes the orchestrator less dependent on a fixed catalog. Against an AWS Agent Registry, it can search approved capabilities with hybrid semantic and keyword search, parse MCP or A2A descriptors, and instantiate request-scoped clients. Governance determines what is discoverable. Authentication remains an explicit concern for the Registry and each invoked capability.

AWS Agent Registry is generally available with capabilities that extend beyond this single-account sample:

  • Organization-wide discovery and cross-account sharing can expose governed records across account boundaries through supported AWS Organizations and sharing mechanisms.
  • Automatic capability synchronization can populate supported descriptors from a URL. Credential-provider configuration on that synchronization request is used to fetch descriptor content. It isn’t returned to runtime consumers as invocation authentication.
  • Approval workflows can use Registry status APIs and IAM permissions to connect CI checks, security review, or human approval to the 
    DRAFT
    → 
    PENDING_APPROVAL
    → 
    APPROVED
    lifecycle.
  • Tagging, AWS CloudFormation support, and infrastructure-as-code patterns can make Registry deployment and governance repeatable. Evaluation should verify search relevance and invocation behavior for the organization’s own catalog.

Run the runtime-discovery sample, then register one compatible MCP server or agent of your own. Confirm that its descriptor, approval state, authentication path, and search behavior match your production requirements.

Learn more

  • AWS Agent Registry general availability announcement
  • AWS Agent Registry documentation
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console (Registry)
  • AWS Agent Registry general availability technical blog post

entries.title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS
entries.summary: Learn how to secure multi-agent AI systems with cryptographic identity using Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS services. This reference architecture combines signed request envelopes, user-signed delegation assertions, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens, and real-time OCSP revocation to prove agent identity and prevent request forgery across agent-to-agent and MCP tool calls.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS

When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand.

Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization.

In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents.

The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK. While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.

About Keyfactor EJBCA

Keyfactor provides a widely adopted machine identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide, according to Keyfactor. These organizations span financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and government. Keyfactor helps organizations establish and maintain cryptographic trust through certificate lifecycle management, PKI operations, and machine identity governance.

EJBCA Enterprise is Keyfactor’s Certificate Authority (CA) and PKI platform, designed for high-availability deployment and REST API automation. Available as an enterprise product, EJBCA provides X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management through both a web console and REST API. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2).

The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments.

Solution overview

The architecture implements three authentication layers, each addressing a different trust boundary in the agent communication chain. These three layers use the four security mechanisms introduced earlier: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation. The mechanisms combine across layers as shown in the following table.

LayerTrust boundaryMechanismValidates
1. User AuthUser to SystemOAuth + X.509 cert + delegation mintingUser identity, credential binding
2. Agent-to-AgentAgent to AgentSigned envelopes (PoP + nonce + timestamp)Caller identity, request freshness, no replay
3. MCP AuthAgent to Tool ServerScoped token + envelope + delegationAll identities, authorization chain, OCSP

Figure 1 shows the three authentication layers and how credentials flow between the user, agents, and the MCP tool server. The diagram illustrates the separation between user credentials (which stay in the login flow), agent credentials (scoped per agent), and the delegation chain that connects them.

Figure 2 illustrates the detailed traffic flow during a typical user session. It shows the sequence of authentication steps from login through certificate issuance, agent delegation, tool invocation, and session cleanup.

AWS services used

The following AWS services form the foundation of the reference architecture.

ServicePurpose
Amazon BedrockLLM inference through Strands Agents SDK
Amazon RDS for MySQLApplication database accessed through MCP tools
Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES)Email delivery for the Email Agent
AWS Secrets ManagerSecure storage for PKCS12 bundles, tokens, and metadata
Amazon EC2Hosts Keycloak IDP and EJBCA PKI server

Solution walkthrough

The following steps walk through each component of the architecture, from initial user login through to session cleanup. Each step builds on the previous one, establishing a chain of trust that connects the human user to the final tool execution.

Prerequisites

  • An active AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, Amazon RDS for MySQL, Amazon SES, and AWS Secrets Manager.
  • Keycloak 26.2 or later (required for RFC 8693 standard token exchange. Previous versions use a legacy exchange that is incompatible).
  • Keyfactor EJBCA Enterprise with REST API V1 and an OCSP responder configured.
  • EJBCA API administrator certificate (
    api-admin.p12
    ) for REST API authentication.
  • Python 3.9+ development environment.
  • Familiarity with X.509 certificates, OCSP, OAuth 2.0, RSA digital signatures, and PKCS#12 key stores.

Step 1: User login, certificate issuance, and delegation minting

The login flow establishes the user’s identity through three mechanisms and then delegates authority to the AI agents without sharing the user’s credentials. This separation is critical: Agents receive proof of authorization without ever holding the user’s private key or full-session OAuth token.

First, the application authenticates the user against Keycloak using an OAuth 2.0 password grant, receiving a full-session access token and refresh token. Immediately after, the application performs an RFC 8693 token exchange to obtain a downscoped token. This token’s audience is restricted to the MCP server. Only this limited token is handed to agents. If it’s inadvertently exposed, it can’t access any other service in the organization.

Second, the application generates an RSA 2048+ key pair locally and submits a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to EJBCA through the 

pkcs10enroll
REST API endpoint. EJBCA signs the CSR and returns the certificate. The application bundles the certificate and private key into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager. The private key never leaves the application boundary. It is not sent to EJBCA, not shared with agents, and not stored on the filesystem. Three agent certificates are issued using the same CSR-based flow, one per agent role.

Third, the user’s private key signs a delegation assertion. This is a JSON document listing the SHA-256 fingerprints of all three agent certificates, along with the user’s subject name, issuance time, and expiry. This delegation proves that the user authorized these specific agents to act on their behalf. Agents carry this delegation instead of the user’s certificate.

Step 2: Agent-to-agent signed envelopes

When the orchestrator agent routes a request to a sub-agent (such as the MySQL agent or Email agent), it does not simply pass its certificate for identification. Instead, it signs the entire request payload, including the tool name, arguments, a timestamp, and a cryptographically random nonce, using its private key with 

RSA-PSS-SHA256
. The resulting signed envelope provides proof-of-possession. The receiving agent can verify that the caller actually holds the private key corresponding to the presented certificate.

The receiving agent performs six validation checks on the envelope before processing the request:

  • Signature verification: Proves the sender possesses the private key (proof-of-possession).
  • Timestamp freshness: The envelope must be within 
    ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS
    (default 60 seconds) of the current time.
  • Nonce uniqueness: The 
    ReplayCache
    rejects any previously seen nonce, preventing request replay.
  • CA chain validation: The sender’s certificate must chain to the trusted CA (
    UserCA.pem
    ).
  • Role authorization: The certificate CN’s role suffix must be in 
    ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES
    for this agent.
  • OCSP revocation check: A real-time check against EJBCA confirms the certificate has not been revoked.

If the orchestrator needs to re-send the same prompt (for example, after a transient failure), it must create a new envelope with a fresh nonce. Old envelopes can’t be replayed, even by the legitimate sender.

Step 3: MCP server authentication

The MCP server (FastMCP) is the final trust boundary before any database operation runs. It performs four validation checks on every tool invocation, implementing defense-in-depth. Even if one credential is subject to unauthorized access, the remaining checks prevent unauthorized operations.

The authentication sequence:

  • Token introspection: A POST to the Keycloak 
    /token/introspect
    endpoint verifies the token is active and its audience contains “mcp-server”. A full-session token without the correct audience is rejected.
  • Envelope verification: The agent’s signed envelope is validated for signature correctness, timestamp freshness, nonce uniqueness, CA chain trust, role match (
    mysql-agent
    ), and OCSP non-revocation.
  • Delegation verification: The user’s delegation assertion is validated. The signature proves the user’s key holder authorized this delegation, the calling agent’s certificate fingerprint appears in the authorized list, and the user’s certificate is checked through OCSP.
  • Identity cross-check: The token username, the delegation subject, and the agent certificate CN prefix must all match. This confirms a single consistent identity chain from user through to tool execution.

Step 4: Replay prevention

Every signed envelope carries a unique nonce, a 128-bit cryptographically random hex string generated with Python’s secrets module. The 

ReplayCache
is a thread-safe in-memory store that remembers every nonce until its freshness window expires (2x 
ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS
). If the same nonce appears in a second request, the envelope is immediately rejected, even if its signature is valid and the timestamp is fresh.

The timestamp validation complements the nonce check. An envelope’s timestamp must be within 

ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS
(default 60 seconds) of the server’s current time. Together, these mechanisms address four unauthorized access scenarios:
  • Recorded replay: An unauthorized user captures a valid envelope and resubmits it later. The nonce was already seen.
  • Delayed delivery: An envelope intercepted in transit arrives after the freshness window. The timestamp check fails.
  • Stale request reuse: An old envelope cached by a proxy is resubmitted. Both nonce and timestamp checks fail.
  • Precomputed forgery: An unauthorized user cannot predict future nonces to pre-sign envelopes.

Step 5: Client-side key generation

A critical security property of this architecture is that private keys are generated locally and never transmitted to any external system. The application generates RSA 2048+ key pairs using the Python cryptography library. It constructs a CSR containing only the public key and subject information, and sends only the CSR to EJBCA through the 

pkcs10enroll
endpoint.

EJBCA validates the CSR, applies the certificate profile (7-day validity, key usage constraints), signs it with the CA key, and returns the issued certificate. The application then bundles the locally held private key with the returned certificate into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager.

This design provides several security properties:

  • The user’s private key is used only at login to sign the delegation assertion. It’s never shared with agents.
  • Each agent’s private key is used only by that agent to sign envelopes. It’s never shared between agents.
  • EJBCA never sees or stores private keys. It operates purely as a certificate authority.
  • If Secrets Manager is subject to unauthorized access, the PKCS12 password (stored separately) adds an additional layer.
  • Key material can be rotated independently by re-enrolling with a new CSR at next login.

Step 6: Complete logout and credential revocation

Logout triggers a revocation cascade that immediately invalidates all outstanding credentials. The sequence results in no remaining valid credentials after completion:

  • Revoke user certificate in EJBCA: This immediately invalidates all outstanding delegations, because delegation verification checks the user’s certificate through OCSP in real time.
  • Revoke all three agent certificates: This invalidates all outstanding signed envelopes, since envelope verification includes OCSP.
  • Delete all secrets from AWS Secrets Manager: Using 
    ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery
    for immediate removal with no recovery window.
  • Terminate Keycloak session: Invalidates the downscoped token through the session termination endpoint.

The revocation cascade is the key security property. Revoking a single user certificate at the PKI layer promptly revokes all downstream agent authority without needing to individually revoke tokens, delete sessions, or contact each agent. OCSP provides the propagation mechanism, and because every request checks OCSP, the effect is immediate.

Security considerations

The design choices in this architecture address several security properties that are important for production multi-agent deployments.

Private key isolation. The user’s private key exists only during the login flow and is used solely to sign the delegation. Agent keys are scoped per-agent and never shared. No key material crosses trust boundaries.

Delegation compared to credential sharing. Agents prove their authority through a cryptographic chain (delegation to agent fingerprint to envelope signature) without ever holding user credentials. If an agent key is exposed, only that agent’s key is revealed, not the user’s.

Audience-scoped tokens. RFC 8693 token exchange produces a token accepted only by the MCP server. An inadvertently disclosed downscoped token cannot authenticate against Keycloak admin APIs, other services, or even a different MCP server instance.

Replay prevention. The combination of per-request nonces and a 60-second freshness window confirms that every request is single-use and time-bound. The 

ReplayCache
is thread-safe and self-cleaning.

Fail-closed design. Every validation failure results in immediate denial. OCSP unreachable: deny. Invalid signature: deny. Expired timestamp: deny. Replayed nonce: deny. Wrong audience: deny. There’s no graceful degradation for security checks.

Revocation cascade. Revoking one user certificate promptly invalidates all delegations, all agent authority, and all outstanding envelopes. This is propagated through real-time OCSP without requiring individual credential cleanup.

Forward-only trust chain. The 

ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES
map enforces that only 
orchestrator-agent
can call 
mysql-agent
and 
email-agent
. Sub-agents cannot call each other, can’t call upward to the orchestrator, and cannot impersonate the user.

AI governance considerations

The PKI architecture provides built-in behavior boundaries for the AI agents in this system. Production deployments should use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering, topic avoidance, and grounding checks on agent responses, alongside the PKI-based access controls described in this post.

  • Tool boundaries: The AI agent operates under strict tool constraints. It can only invoke pre-defined MCP tools (
    execute_sql
    , 
    describe_table
    , 
    list_tables
    ). The agent can’t execute arbitrary code or access resources outside its certificate scope.
  • Human oversight: All agent actions are logged and auditable. AWS CloudTrail captures AWS API calls, and the MCP server logs every validated tool invocation with the full identity chain (user, agent, timestamp, and operation).
  • Data handling: User queries and results stay within the authenticated session boundary. The audience-scoped token confines data access to the specific MCP server instance.
  • Certificate-based behavior boundaries: Agents can only invoke tools they hold valid certificates for. An agent without a 
    mysql-agent
    certificate cannot access the database, regardless of what the LLM might generate as instructions.

Extending the architecture

You can extend this architecture to support additional agent types, horizontal scaling, and multi-tenant isolation. The following paragraphs describe the most common extension points.

  • To add new agent types, you only need to add an entry in 
    ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES
    . Certificates are automatically issued at login, and the delegation assertion dynamically includes the new agent’s fingerprint. No infrastructure changes are required.
  • For horizontal scaling, you can deploy EJBCA’s OCSP responder in high-availability mode behind a load balancer. AWS Secrets Manager supports high request rates suitable for this workload. The 
    ReplayCache
    can be backed by Amazon ElastiCache for distributed deployments.
  • To harden the architecture for production, you can use hardware security module (HSM)-backed EJBCA signing keys through AWS CloudHSM or an on-premises HSM. OCSP response stapling reduces validation latency, and Certificate Transparency logs provide a full audit trail of issued certificates.
  • For multi-tenant deployments, you can create per-tenant Certificate Authorities or per-tenant delegation authorities for cryptographic tenant isolation. Combined with per-tenant AWS accounts, this delivers strong isolation between tenants.
  • You can also complement PKI-based agent identity with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Use PKI for agent-to-agent authentication and IAM for AWS service authorization. The two systems work independently, providing defense in depth.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, remove the resources created during this walkthrough:

  • Delete the Amazon RDS for MySQL instance (or the AWS CloudFormation stack if you used the scripted setup).
  • Delete all secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, including user certificates and agent certificates under the 
    mcp/
    prefix.
  • Remove the verified sender email address from Amazon SES.
  • Terminate the Amazon EC2 instances running Keycloak and EJBCA (if deployed for this demonstration).
  • Revoke and delete all test certificates in EJBCA by using the EJBCA admin console or REST API.
  • Remove the Keycloak realm (
    mcp-realm
    ) and associated clients.
  • If you used the scripted setup, run 
    ./scripts/cleanup.sh
    (Linux) or 
    ./scripts/cleanup.bat
    (Windows) to automate these steps.

Conclusion

In this post, we demonstrated a reference architecture for securing AI agent communications using X.509 PKI with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS services. The architecture addresses the fundamental identity gap in multi-agent AI systems through four complementary mechanisms:

  • Signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every inter-agent call, making it significantly harder for an unauthorized party to forge an agent’s identity or replay its requests.
  • User-signed delegation assertions decouple authorization from credential sharing. Agents prove they are authorized to act on the user’s behalf without holding the user’s private key or full-session token.
  • RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any token disclosure to a single service boundary.
  • Real-time OCSP revocation checking confirms that credential revocation takes immediate effect across the entire system. Revoking one user certificate promptly ends all downstream agent authority.

This architecture is framework-agnostic. While we demonstrated it with the AWS Strands Agents SDK and FastMCP, the same PKI patterns apply to LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, or any other multi-agent framework that uses tool protocols. As AI agents proliferate and gain access to increasingly sensitive operations, agent identity infrastructure moves from optional to essential.

To get started with this reference architecture, see the accompanying GitHub repository. For more information about the services used, see the following resources:

entries.title: How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Learn how Eon replaced per-tool credentials and local MCP processes across AWS, GCP, and Azure with a single authenticated Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway, giving more than 100 developers and autonomous agents unified access to production investigation and cutting new-engineer onboarding from two days to two minutes.
entries.content:

How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

This is a guest post co-written with Roei Zavida from Eon.

Independent software vendors (ISVs) building AI-powered products need to connect agents and humans to dozens of operational tools across clouds, each with different authentication models, network boundaries, and access policies. When those tools span AWS, GCP, and Azure simultaneously, the integration surface multiplies.

This post describes how Eon used Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Eon used it to replace per-tool credentials and local Model Context Protocol (MCP) processes with a single authenticated gateway. The result gives developers and autonomous agents unified access to investigation tooling across three clouds. New engineers now reach all their investigation tools in about two minutes instead of the two days it previously took to configure credentials and local MCP servers.

About Eon

Eon provides the Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era. The platform discovers and classifies cloud resources across AWS, Azure, and GCP. It provides continuous deduplicated backup that reduces storage costs by up to 50 percent in Eon’s internal measurements. It also detects ransomware and rogue-agent damage and delivers live grounded context for AI agents. All of this runs from a single read-only AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, storing data in Apache Parquet and Apache Iceberg formats. Founded by former AWS engineers, Eon runs its software as a service (SaaS) infrastructure on AWS.

The challenge

Eon’s internal engineering team investigates production incidents across multiple clouds and dozens of operational systems. A crashed Kubernetes pod requires checking container logs, Grafana metrics, the deployment’s GitHub pull request (PR), and cloud-provider health status within the same session.

Eon needed to address several key requirements:

  • Credential consolidation — Each new tool added another integration to configure, secure, and rotate, which got harder to keep consistent as the toolset grew.
  • Eliminate local MCP processes — Each developer ran several MCP servers locally, which was hard to standardize and keep current.
  • Identity separation — Engineers accessed each system with role-based permissions, but there was no single place to decide which tools each person or agent could call.
  • Cross-account access without networking overhead — Hosting MCP servers across multiple AWS accounts required virtual private cloud (VPC) peering or AWS PrivateLink per account, multiplying operational cost and setup time.
  • Developer onboarding — New engineers spent roughly 2 days configuring credentials and local MCP servers before investigating their first incident.
  • Agent access — Eon’s autonomous site reliability engineering (SRE) agent (running Claude on Amazon Bedrock) needed the same tool access as humans, but with different permissions.

Growing engineering headcount combined with a fast-expanding set of AI tools and MCPs made maintaining credentials and local MCP servers increasingly costly. This pushed Eon toward a centralized solution.

Approaches considered

Before building on AgentCore, Eon evaluated alternatives:

Option 1: Centralized proxy with custom auth

Every harness had its own proxy configuration with all the targets. A single reverse proxy aggregating all tools, with a custom authentication layer. This handled credential consolidation but only supported remote MCP and required building and maintaining tool protocol translation, session management, and authorization logic from scratch. The implementation and maintenance burden was significant.

Option 2: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is a managed gateway with built-in identity federation, Cedar-based authorization policies, and Runtime hosting that converts local MCP servers to remote HTTP endpoints. This addressed all requirements without custom infrastructure.

Eon chose Option 2 because it provided identity separation, cross-account connectivity, and policy enforcement as managed capabilities rather than code they would need to build and maintain. These were the only two options on the table.

Solution overview

Eon deployed the full Amazon Bedrock AgentCore stack: AgentCore Gateway, Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AgentCore Runtime, and AgentCore Identity, all capabilities of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram shows how client requests flow through the authentication layer to a single gateway. The gateway routes authorized tool calls to targets hosted on AgentCore Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts.

The architecture has five layers:

Clients

Developers using Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenAI Codex connect to a single MCP URL. An autonomous SRE agent running Claude on Amazon Bedrock connects to the same gateway with a different identity.

Identity plane

Corporate single sign-on (SSO) federates through Amazon Cognito, which mints the JSON Web Token (JWT) and hands it to the gateway. Amazon API Gateway sits in front as the OAuth entry point for humans, proxying the MCP session. Agents authenticate with Cognito 

client_credentials
grants directly against the gateway.

One gateway, least-privilege access

A single AgentCore MCP Gateway serves as the company-wide front door. Cedar policies in ENFORCE mode control which principals can invoke which tools. Read operations are available to selected groups, not every authenticated user. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only.

Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Cedar policies map each principal to permitted tools. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only. The gateway evaluates every 

tools/call
request against Cedar before forwarding to the target.

Targets

Dozens of target MCP servers exposing hundreds of tools on the one gateway, served by AgentCore Runtimes distributed across multiple AWS accounts. Each Runtime converts local stdio-based MCP servers into Streamable HTTP endpoints accessible through the gateway.

A developer opens their integrated development environment (IDE), configures one MCP URL, authenticates through corporate SSO, and the gateway aggregates hundreds of tools into a single 

tools/list
response. No local setup and no per-tool tokens.

Identity and access separation

The core security decision was enforcing read and write boundaries through Cedar policy at the gateway level.

Single gateway, policy-enforced separation:

The gateway accepts both JWT tokens (humans through corporate SSO and Cognito) and 

client_credentials
tokens (agents). Cedar policies determine what each principal can do. Humans in approved groups get read access. Write operations require explicit Cedar permits granted only to specific agent identities.

Cedar reinforces per-tool granularity:

Cedar policies are managed as code through GitHub PRs with review comments, giving the team version control and audit trail on every permission change.

Within the gateway, Cedar policies scope tool access by SSO group, and groups map to job role. Engineers have access to development and testing environments by default. Production access follows Eon’s security and compliance controls: it is read-only, granted just-in-time through an approval process, and audited. A new team member’s group is scoped the same way, by role rather than by which service they happen to own. Because every agent action is checked against Cedar in ENFORCE mode and scoped to a least-privilege tool set, the autonomous agent operates within safe, bounded limits. It can only invoke the specific tools its identity is explicitly permitted to call.

“Before, our internal agent couldn’t reach the same investigation tools developers used. After, it uses the same Gateway with its own identity and a tighter tool set.”

— Roei Zavida, Senior DevOps Engineer, Eon

Cross-account connectivity

Eon runs Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts, organized by environment or service boundary. AgentCore Gateway reaches each Runtime through IAM cross-account role assumption. The Runtime in Account B trusts the AgentCore Gateway execution role in Account A through a standard IAM trust policy.

What this eliminated:

  • VPC peering configuration and route table management across multiple AWS accounts.
  • PrivateLink endpoint costs per account.
  • Security group coordination between accounts.
  • Days of setup per new account (replaced by one IAM trust policy, deployable in minutes).

Target attachment patterns:

Depending on each tool’s authentication and hosting model, Eon uses two primary attachment patterns. The following table summarizes when to use each pattern and gives an example.

PatternWhen to useExample
Runtime + IAMTool needs a cloud hop through IAM credentialsGrafana queries, Kubernetes API calls
Runtime wrapping remote MCPTool surface needs filtering or credential translationLinear

Most targets use Runtime + IAM. Eon only wraps a remote MCP to shrink its catalog or slot in a credential the gateway cannot otherwise supply.

Investigation session flow

The following flow traces a developer investigating a production incident:

  • Authentication. The developer opens Claude Code (or Cursor/Codex) and connects to the gateway MCP URL. The IDE initiates OAuth through corporate SSO. Cognito issues a JWT carrying the developer’s identity and group memberships.
  • Tool discovery. The gateway aggregates `tools/list` from dozens of connected targets and returns a unified manifest of hundreds of tools to the IDE. The developer sees all available investigation tools in one list.
  • Tool invocation. The developer asks: “Show me the error rate spike for the payments service in the last hour.” The IDE’s agent selects the Grafana query tool and sends a `tools/call` request.
  • Policy evaluation. The gateway evaluates the request against Cedar. The developer’s group membership grants access to the Grafana tool. The request passes.
  • Runtime execution. The gateway forwards the request to the Runtime hosting the Grafana MCP server (running in a separate AWS account). The Runtime authenticates to Grafana using a service credential stored in the AgentCore Identity vault, executes the query, and returns results.
  • Cross-tool correlation. The agent follows up by checking the Kubernetes deployment status and the related GitHub PR, each routed to different Runtimes. The developer sees correlated results without switching tools or re-authenticating.

Lessons learned at scale

Deploying to 100+ developers and approximately 10,000 sessions surfaced production challenges:

Managing Cedar policy size

Every tool schema that the gateway pre-indexes contributes to Cedar policy size. With dozens of targets exposing extensive tool manifests, Eon’s policy grew toward the size quota. The fix: DYNAMIC listing mode for high-tool-count targets. In DYNAMIC mode, the gateway forwards 

tools/list
calls to the MCP server at request time instead of pre-indexing schemas, adding zero bytes to the policy.

The trade-off is that semantic tool search is unavailable for DYNAMIC targets. Eon runs a hybrid configuration: DEFAULT mode for targets requiring per-user OAuth (smaller tool counts, need pre-indexed schemas for the consent flow) and DYNAMIC mode for large-catalog targets.

OAuth session binding for standard MCP clients

Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex expect the OAuth 

state
parameter for cross-site request forgery (CSRF) protection. AgentCore uses session-URI binding. Eon built an Amazon API Gateway shim that translates between the two protocols so standard MCP clients can complete the OAuth flow without modification.

Filtering tool surfaces

Some MCP servers expose hundreds of tools. Individual developers need only a subset for their service. Eon built a Runtime wrapper that filters the tool manifest at the Runtime layer, reducing noise in 

tools/list
responses and preventing accidental invocation of irrelevant operations. This approach also keeps those targets on DEFAULT mode, preserving semantic search and embedded features that DYNAMIC mode sacrifices.

Results

MetricBefore AgentCoreAfter AgentCore
Credential sets per developerOne per system/MCP server (GitHub, Grafana, cloud accounts, etc.)0 (one SSO login)
Local MCP processes per machine100
Developer onboarding time2 days2 minutes
Cross-account networking configsVPC peering per account0 (IAM-only)
Tool authorizationConfigured per toolOne Cedar policy for humans and agents
Developers on the platform—100+
Tools accessible from one URL—Hundreds (across dozens of targets)
Sessions processed—~10,000

The single-gateway architecture has run in production for Eon’s internal engineering team for several months. The clearest outcome is developer onboarding. Setting up access to the full tool set dropped from roughly two days of configuring credentials and local MCP servers to about two minutes. A new engineer connects one gateway URL, authenticates through corporate SSO, and immediately sees the tools their role allows.

The internal agent accounts for most of the time saved, because it gains access to more context through the gateway, improving investigation accuracy. Engineers save the time previously spent on AI tool setup, because they only need to connect to the gateway URL.

Eon is exploring how the same patterns can support AI capabilities in its own product.

“AgentCore gave us one authenticated MCP Gateway instead of per-tool tokens and local MCP processes. Developers and our internal agent now reach Kubernetes, Grafana, GitHub, and our cloud accounts from a single URL.”

— Roei Zavida, Senior DevOps Engineer, Eon

Conclusion

This post described how Eon replaced per-tool credentials and local MCP processes with a single Amazon Bedrock AgentCore MCP Gateway. The result is Cedar-based identity separation, cross-account connectivity without VPC peering, and unified tool access for more than 100 developers and autonomous agents across three clouds. The single-gateway architecture, Cedar least-privilege enforcement, and hybrid DEFAULT and DYNAMIC policy mode are reusable patterns for ISVs connecting agents and developers to tools across multiple clouds.

To learn more about building on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, review these resources:

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway documentation.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime documentation.
  • Getting Started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Workshop.

entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Agentic AI applications need governed access to live enterprise data. That data can live in operational systems, analytical warehouses, SaaS applications, other clouds, or on premises. In the previous post in this series, we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. A Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore queried that layer. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post uses the same customer 360 pattern, but swaps in a different semantic layer implementation and extends the source mix.

Two things change here. First, the semantic layer is the Denodo Platform: an AI data layer that provides active context and live, zero-copy access to distributed enterprise data. The agent talks to it in VQL, Denodo’s SQL dialect. Second, the source mix includes an on-premises PostgreSQL database alongside Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift, so the federation problem is no longer bounded by an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC).

The rest of the pattern carries over. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock plans and writes queries. The Denodo MCP Server exposes governed views to the agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent, terminates inbound authentication, and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to Denodo. Everything the model reasons over lives inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt: the joins, the metric definitions, and the row and column filters that apply to the caller.

By the end of this post, you will know:

  • How to federate Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and an on-premises PostgreSQL database in Denodo into a single customer 360 view an agent can query.
  • How to expose that semantic view to an AgentCore-hosted agent through the Denodo MCP Server, and how to register the MCP Server as an AgentCore Gateway target.
  • How the end user’s identity flows from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity On-Behalf-Of token exchange to Denodo.
  • How Global Security Policies apply row and column filters at query time.
  • The two deployment options for Denodo on AWS: Agora, the fully managed cloud service, and self-managed installation on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS).

We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the previous post: what it is, what it’s for, and why the model plans query without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the previous post covers the ground.

The example: Customer 360 with a source outside AWS

We stay with the same customer 360 pattern from the previous post. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit used in the previous article models an ecommerce retailer with two motivating use cases: understanding churn and identifying customers for auto-enrollment in a rewards program. The schema doesn’t change in this post. What changes is where one table lives: 

rewards_account
sits on an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster rather than in Amazon Aurora with the rest of the customer profile data.

That placement isn’t a special case. Enterprise data sources might be outside AWS: on premises, in a SaaS tool like a CRM, or in another cloud. The semantic layer must reach whichever applies. We use on-premises PostgreSQL for the walkthrough that represents data from a third-party application. The Extending to other sources section covers what changes when the source is a SaaS tool, a CRM, or a mainframe. It also covers the other hundreds of data sources that Denodo supports by default.

Amazon Aurora (PostgreSQL-compatible): Customer profile

TableKey columns
customercid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location
addressid (PK), city, state, zip, street_name
credit_cardid (PK), cid, card_num, card_type

Amazon Redshift: Order history

TableKey columns
orderid (PK), cid, pid, order_date, quantity, price, card
productid (PK), name, brand, price, dept

On-premises PostgreSQL: Rewards program

TableKey columns
rewards_accountid (PK), cid, account_id, create_date

The shared identifier is 

cid
, a plain integer that appears as the primary key in the Aurora customer table. It appears as a non-foreign-key column in the Amazon Redshift order table and the on-premises 
rewards_account
. Within Aurora itself, the 
customer.location
column is an integer foreign key to 
address.id
, which is how the profile joins to the address record. There is no foreign key that spans two engines, and no ETL job to build one. Answers that join customers to their purchases and their rewards enrollment must reconcile 
cid
at query time.

A representative question this setup answers: “Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?” This is the auto-enrollment scenario from the Stardog kit, and it needs profile data from Aurora, lifetime spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from the on-premises cluster to answer.

Denodo plans the federated query at execution time, deciding what to push into Aurora, what to push into Amazon Redshift, what to fetch from the on-premises cluster, and how to combine the results. No data moves between sources, and the semantic layer stays declared once for every consumer to reuse.

Denodo terms used in this post

Denodo implements the semantic layer as a data virtualization platform. Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) is the query engine at the core: it’s where the semantic-layer objects live, where VQL executes, and where access policies evaluate. Design Studio is the browser-based authoring surface for VDP. Every object modeled in this post is defined there.

Three object types come up repeatedly.

  • A base view is a mapping between a physical table, API, or file in a source system and a logical view in VDP. One Aurora table maps to one base view.
  • A derived view is a VQL query over one or more base or other derived views. The 
    customer_360
    view in this post is a derived view.
  • A metric view defines a business measure once (for example, 
    lifetime_customer_value
    ) and lets other derived views reference it. Metric views separate the definition of a measure from any specific query that uses it.

VQL is Denodo’s SQL dialect. It’s ANSI-aligned SQL plus a set of Denodo-specific constructs, notably DDL constructs to represent data sources and syntax for semantic metric views. In an agentic scenario, the specific syntax of VQL is provided by a skill that will be used by the LLM when using Denodo tools to facilitate correct use of Denodo’s syntax.

A Global Security Policy (GSP) is a runtime access-control rule that applies to views or columns carrying a specific tag. GSPs are how row filters and column masks get enforced at query time, evaluated per caller.

For a fuller reference, see the Denodo Platform documentation.

Reference architecture

The runtime has two flows. Inbound: A client sends the user’s request to the agent through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent process. The agent invokes a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in this walkthrough) to interpret the prompt and plan the query.

Outbound: AgentCore Gateway also acts as the outbound proxy for the agent’s tool calls. The Denodo MCP Server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls the agent makes for enterprise data route through Gateway to the MCP Server. Before the request reaches Denodo, AgentCore Identity performs an On-Behalf-Of token exchange, converting the human user’s inbound token into a scoped access token that represents the same user with Denodo as the audience. The Denodo MCP Server accepts the exchanged token as a bearer credential and forwards the VQL request to Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) over JDBC. VDP validates the token independently, resolves the caller to a Denodo role, applies access policies, and plans the federated query against Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises PostgreSQL cluster.

Only the VQL request travels down to VDP and the result set travels back up. No source data moves between engines. Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises cluster respond to native SQL rewritten by VDP’s federated optimizer. The following sections cover the identity propagation and policy enforcement in detail. Additional sections cover the MCP Server registration and agent deployment steps.

Build the semantic layer

The semantic model in Denodo is not a single artifact. It’s a collection of base views, derived views, metric views, and tags in VDP that together present business-meaningful data to consumers. Building the semantic model in this post means creating each of those pieces.

We build in three passes: base views over each source table, a derived view (

customer_360
) that joins the base views on 
cid
at the customer level, and a metric view (
lifetime_customer_value
) that defines a reusable spend aggregation queries can join in when they need it.

In practice, this modeling is done visually in Denodo Design Studio. You drag Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises PostgreSQL source onto a canvas, draw joins between them, and rename or re-type fields (for example, mapping 

cust_ref
to 
customer_id
) through a form rather than hand-written DDL. Attaching the security policies covered later in this post also happens inside the same UI.

Metric views live beside the derived views that reference them, defined once and reused. If two teams build two different customer-level views over the same base data, both surface the same metric definitions.

Base views

Each source table becomes a base view in VDP. For the Aurora customer table, that means introducing Aurora using the specific connector in Design Studio, pointing at the schema, and letting VDP introspect the columns. Design Studio handles the introspection. The resulting base view is a one-to-one mapping between the physical columns and their VDP counterparts, and it doesn’t transform the source data.

Two additional configurations happen during creation:

  • Column tags for governance. 
    ssn
    on the base view over customer gets the tag 
    pii_sensitive
    . 
    card_num
    on the base view over 
    credit_card
    gets the same tag. These tags are what the Global Security Policy defined in the Governed access section binds to.
  • Primary keys and join fields. 
    cid
    is marked as the primary key on 
    aurora_customer
    and as the join field on 
    redshift_order
    and 
    postgres_rewards_account
    . Design Studio infers primary keys from source metadata when it’s available. Otherwise, you set them once in the base view definition.

Repeat for the source tables introduced earlier. Six base views result: 

aurora_customer
, 
aurora_address
, and 
aurora_credit_card
over Amazon Aurora; 
redshift_order
and 
redshift_product
over Amazon Redshift; and 
postgres_rewards_account
over on-premises PostgreSQL.

Design Studio also supports natural-language authoring through Denodo Assistant. A developer can describe a view in plain English (for example, “join customer profile from Aurora with order totals from Amazon Redshift on 

cid
”) and get back a candidate VQL definition to review and refine in the same canvas before saving. Refinement is iterative: follow-up prompts adjust filters, joins, or field mappings before the definition is finalized. The governance and typing rules described in this section still apply to objects created this way.

Derived view: The customer 360

customer_360
is the customer-level view across the three sources, with one row per customer. Order details and aggregations live separately, in the metric view we define next.

Two properties of this definition matter for the rest of the architecture. First, the joins live in Denodo Platform rather than in a pipeline. There is no ETL job maintaining a materialized 

customer_360
table. VDP resolves the joins at execution time: Aurora returns the profile plus card, the on-premises cluster returns the rewards enrollment record, and VDP combines them on 
cid
. Second, the derived view carries every column, including 
ssn
and 
card_num
.

For governance and AI, we also add metadata: column tags for personally identifiable information (PII) fields, and descriptions that document the view and each field. Denodo’s Assistant can use an LLM to suggest these. Later sections show why this metadata matters.

Metric view: Lifetime customer value

Metric views define reusable business measures with a specific SOURCES/DIMENSIONS/METRICS structure. See the Defining a Metric View reference in the VQL guide for the full syntax. 

lifetime_customer_value
doesn’t live inside 
customer_360
. It lives beside it, as its own object:

Other views and external reporting tools can reference 

lifetime_customer_value
the same way it references other views. When a business rule changes (say, 
lifetime_spend
should exclude canceled orders), the update happens once in the metric definition. Every consumer picks up the change at the next query, without touching the derived view or the downstream application. Different teams can stand up their own derived views to convey the way their line of business sees the world. The base data stays shared while the semantic interpretation stays independent, so neither team’s edits disturb the other.

How VDP executes the federated query

When the agent runs the auto-enrollment question from The example (“Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?”), the corresponding VQL uses the metric view to compute the result set and evaluate the desired metric:

Although this query only references the metric view, VDP’s cost-based optimizer plans the federated execution across the three engines where the corresponding data is originating. The resulting plan looks approximately like this:

  • Push down to Amazon Aurora: Denodo pushes a join of customer, address, and 
    credit_card
    to Aurora, returning customer profile fields including 
    first_name
    , 
    last_name
    , state, and 
    cid
    .
  • Push down to on-premises PostgreSQL: Denodo pushes a projection of 
    rewards_account
    returning 
    cid
    and 
    create_date
    .
  • Push down to Amazon Redshift: Denodo pushes the spend aggregation to Amazon Redshift as 
    SUM(price * quantity)
    grouped by 
    cid
    .
  • Combine inside Denodo: Denodo left-joins the Aurora profile result with the PostgreSQL rewards result on 
    cid
    , then right-outer-joins that result with the Amazon Redshift aggregated spend on 
    cid
    . Denodo filters rows where 
    rewards_since
    IS NULL, evaluates the metric as the outer grouped aggregation (
    sum(sum) AS lifetime_spend
    ) grouped by 
    first_name
    , 
    last_name
    , and state, orders by 
    lifetime_spend
    descending, and returns up to 20 rows.

The plan reflects the strengths of each source. Amazon Redshift does the aggregation, Aurora does the customer-profile join because all three profile tables live there, and the on-premises cluster returns a small set of rewards records. VDP handles the final cross-engine join and the top-N filter, working with three compact intermediate result sets that carry one row per customer rather than one row per order. A hand-written pipeline usually approximates this same shape and then must keep it in sync forever.

VDP also handles type reconciliation where it’s cheapest. If the same identifier is stored as an integer in one source and a string in another, VDP pushes the cast into the source that can still filter on the resulting predicate, rather than pulling data across engines and reconciling types afterward.

Beyond query push-down and on-demand federation, VDP also offers caching, aggregate-aware acceleration, and point-to-point replication. These techniques complement push-down capabilities in use cases where pre-calculating complex transformations may be necessary, while preserving access control rules and data lineage.

Publish for discovery

A semantic view that only exists as a queryable endpoint leaves a discoverability gap. The next team that needs a “customer lifetime value” measure has no way to know 

lifetime_customer_value
already exists, what it’s built on, or who else depends on it. Publishing 
customer_360
and 
lifetime_customer_value
to the Denodo Data Marketplace turns them into reusable, governed enterprise data products and closes that gap: both objects appear with their VQL definitions, ownership, business descriptions, custom properties, and lineage back to the base views. Consumers search by business meaning rather than by knowing the schema. The Denodo Data Marketplace also provides other features focused on self-service for non-technical users, including data preparation wizards, endorsements and deprecations notes from the administrators, and the capability to make requests and ask questions to data product owners.

Denodo extends this with the 360 graph, a relationship view around a business concept. This graph attaches the reports, dashboards, notebooks, or agent tools that already use 

customer_360
, along with glossaries that define the meaning of the data in the table or conditions of use, for instance. Consumers can inspect the surrounding context of the dataset before writing a query.

A note on interoperability

The semantic model in Denodo is defined in VQL, but Denodo natively exposes any view over multiple open protocols. The same 

customer_360
view can be reached as SQL through JDBC, ODBC, or ADBC, as GraphQL through the Denodo GraphQL Service, as OData 2.0 or 4.0 through the Denodo OData Service, or as MCP tools through the Denodo MCP Server. Choosing MCP for this walkthrough is a fit for AgentCore. The same view is available to a Power BI dashboard, a Tableau workbook, or a Java application without additional modeling.

Denodo also joined Apache Ossie (incubating), formerly Open Semantic Interchange (OSI), in March 2026, a vendor-neutral open-source specification for semantic metadata. Apache Ossie is at an early stage, but the intent is portability of semantic definitions across applications that adopt it. That said, Denodo already offers integration through Denodo Connects to share metadata with other data catalogs such as SageMaker Catalog, Collibra, Purview, and others.

Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement

Broad reach across data sources is one of the core characteristics of an enterprise-wide semantic layer, but that same reach creates a real risk when runtime access control is missing. If per-user filtering lives in the agent’s code, it’s one prompt injection away from being bypassed. If it lives in the LLM, it doesn’t really live anywhere. If it is enforced only in individual source systems, policies can be inconsistent and may not account for business meaning created across sources. Aurora doesn’t know what “top spender” means in the semantic layer, and neither does an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster behind a bastion host. And very often, especially in hybrid scenarios that blend on-premises and cloud systems, Identity Providers across all of them are not even an option.

The approach in this architecture is to enforce access at the semantic layer, using the identity of the human user who initiated the request, propagated end-to-end from the IdP through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to Denodo Virtual DataPort.

The identity propagation chain

Figure 6 zooms into the identity portion of the reference architecture in Figure 1, expanding the outbound path from the app to Denodo VDP into an eight-hop sequence. The following numbered steps correspond one-to-one to the numbered arrows in the figure.

  • The user authenticates to the app against the enterprise IdP. The IdP returns a JWT carrying the user’s identity and attribute claims — role, region, department, and whatever else the IdP is configured to emit.
  • The app calls the agent through AgentCore Gateway with the user’s JWT as the bearer token.
  • Gateway routes the request to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent process.
  • When the agent invokes an outbound tool call, AgentCore Identity performs an On-Behalf-Of token exchange and returns a new access token whose sub claim is the human user and whose aud claim is Denodo.
  • The agent presents the new access token to the Denodo MCP Server as 
    Authorization: Bearer
    on the MCP request.
  • Denodo VDP validates the JWT against the configured JWKS URL, checks the issuer and audience, extracts the scope claim, and maps the caller to a Denodo role.
  • VDP evaluates Global Security Policies at query time and returns a filtered result set to the agent.
  • VDP queries the data sources to satisfy the request and combines the results before returning them.

Gateway JWT validation at step 2 is optional because VDP re-validates the token in step 6. With Gateway validation on, malformed tokens fail earlier in the request path.

The token exchange at step 4 uses either the RFC 8693 token-exchange grant or the RFC 7523 JWT-bearer grant, based on the credential provider configuration. The credential itself does not enter agent code. AgentCore Identity injects it at call time.

The caller-identity passthrough option at step 8 is enabled per data source and requires Denodo and the source to share the same IdP. When it applies, the caller’s identity is forwarded end-to-end, giving full auditing at the source.

Applying access policies in Denodo

Customer 360 data is regulated. For example, some users (HR, fraud analysts) may need to see PII like a Social Security number (SSN) and full credit card number. But most users (marketing, analytics) must not.

Denodo’s mechanism for this is Global Security Policies with attribute- and role-based access control. A Global Security Policy is a rule that applies to views or columns carrying a specific tag, evaluated against the caller’s role and session attributes at query time. The underlying view is not restructured.

To illustrate this, we’ve tagged two columns (

ssn
and 
card_num
) as PII on the base views over Aurora. We create a Global Security Policy 
mask_pii_columns
.
  • Audience: The caller’s role is not 
    hr_user
    .
  • Elements: Applies to columns with the 
    pii_sensitive
    tag.
  • Action: Mask with asterisks (
    ****
    ).

We then define two Denodo roles.

  • hr_user
    : Has Execute on 
    customer_360
    . Sees every column.
  • marketing_user
    : Has Execute on 
    customer_360
    . Will see 
    ssn
    and 
    card_num
    as 
    ****
    because the policy applies.

When 

marketing_user
runs the VQL query:

VDP evaluates the Global Security Policy before planning the query. It sees that 

ssn
carries the 
pii_sensitive
tag and the caller’s role is not 
hr_user
, so it rewrites the projection to return 
***
for 
ssn
.

For row-level filtering (a US-East analyst who should only see east-coast customers, for example) the same mechanism scales. The policy condition can even depend on session attributes mapped from the JWT token, or pulled dynamically from an external table.

A note on Responsible AI

Denodo’s Global Security Policies filter PII at the semantic layer, so the model never sees 

ssn
or 
card_num
for callers who shouldn’t. Even then, agent responses can echo customer identifiers, locations, or spending patterns in natural language. Treat agent outputs with the same handling and retention policy you apply to the underlying regulated data: scope logging and transcript storage, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content and sensitive-topic controls, and limit who can read the responses. For broader guidance, see Responsible AI in Amazon Bedrock.

Audit and observability across layers

Each layer of the request path logs independently. AgentCore runtime emits invocation records to Amazon CloudWatch. AgentCore Gateway logs inbound MCP requests, including the caller’s JWT sub claim. The Denodo MCP Server records tool calls to its own log. Denodo VDP’s audit log captures the full VQL request, the mapped Denodo role, the resolved federated plan, and policy evaluation outcomes.

These logs can also be incorporated into Amazon CloudWatch. When per-source audit tied to the human user is required (for HIPAA or SOX compliance, for example), configure pass-through session credentials on the base views for those sources so Denodo forwards the caller’s identity to the source system where the source supports it, instead of relying on service accounts.

Expose the layer through the Denodo MCP Server

The Denodo MCP Server is an add-on component that sits between MCP clients and VDP: download the distribution, extract it, edit 

config/application.properties
, and start it. The server listens for streamable HTTP MCP requests at 
http://:8080//mcp
and forwards them to VDP over JDBC.

Three configuration values matter for this walkthrough.

  • mcp.security.oauth2.enabled=true
    : accepts OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens on inbound MCP requests. Paired with VDP’s OAuth authenticator configuration, the token forwards to VDP for validation and role resolution (see also the Governed access section).
  • vdp.datasource.jdbcUrl=jdbc:vdb://:9999/
    : the JDBC URL where VDP is reached. The specific database targeted per request comes from the MCP endpoint path.
  • mcp.visibility.tags=mcp
    controls which views are visible from the MCP Server. If defined, only views tagged with at least one of these tags will be visible.

The server implements the MCP OAuth 2.0 authorization flow, including RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata and RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration.

A note on IdP compatibility

The Denodo MCP Server documents support for the automatic Dynamic Client Registration flow with Okta, Ping Identity, and Keycloak. For other identity providers, the MCP Server also accepts manual client configuration where the OAuth token is obtained out of band and forwarded as a static 

Authorization
header on the MCP request, as described in the Denodo MCP Server User Manual.

Front the server with an Application Load Balancer

If the Denodo MCP Server runs on Amazon EC2 or Amazon EKS in the same VPC as VDP, expose it through an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager. This gives AgentCore Gateway a stable HTTPS endpoint and offloads TLS termination from the MCP Server process. Target group: HTTP, port 8080. The health check path should accept both 200 and 404 as healthy responses, since the root path returns 404 and 

/health
returns 200 when the server is up and connected to VDP.

Register as an AgentCore Gateway target

The full step-by-step walkthrough, including AgentCore Gateway creation, IAM service role configuration, and Gateway target validation, is in Denodo’s Integrating Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Denodo via MCP Server integration guide.

Add Denodo VQL skill in the harness

The Denodo VQL skill acts as a system prompt extension for the LLM within the agent framework (such as Strands or Bedrock AgentCore). When registered in the agent harness, it instructs the model on VQL syntax rules and how to help prevent SQL errors.

Deploy and run the agent

The Denodo AgentCore documentation reference has the full agent code in the Denodo KB. The pattern is short: a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock, an MCP client pointed at the Denodo MCP Server, and an AgentCore runtime entrypoint that wires them together.

Verification
